operations.evidence: The golden thread supports legal compliance and management of building safety.
Keeping records does not by itself demonstrate compliant or effective safety management.
Fire and Rescue Services, BSR and building-control bodies may use golden-thread information.
Potential regulator use does not mean a regulator has reviewed a particular record.
Building information must be kept digitally and secure from unauthorised access.
A digital system is not necessarily secure without control evidence.
Information must be available when needed and presented in a usable way.
Technical availability does not prove that information is complete or understandable.
The record should operate as the building's single source of truth.
A designated system may still contain conflicting, stale or incomplete entries.
Information should be accessible in a simple, understandable format and written in plain English.
Plain language does not remove the need for technical detail where safety decisions depend on it.
Management and storage of the information must comply with GDPR.
A statement of compliance is not evidence of lawful processing in every instance.
The client must keep information describing the building and showing how building work complies with building regulations and duties.
A record of intended compliance is not proof that completed work complies.
The client must share building information with every designer and contractor on the project.
A sharing obligation does not prove receipt, understanding or use.
The client's digital record-keeping system should use version control so changes can be seen.
Version history does not guarantee the correctness of each version.
The record-keeping system supports documents including plans, competence declarations, control plans, compliance statements and occurrence-reporting plans.
Document presence does not prove approval, competence or compliance.
At completion, building information must be handed to the relevant accountable or responsible person and receipt in a usable format confirmed.
A handover confirmation does not prove the recipient validated every document.
APs and PAPs must keep the health and safety file, safety case report, residents' engagement strategy and mandatory occurrence reporting system information.
Record retention does not establish that the underlying duties are performed effectively.
Building information must be provided on request to BSR, other accountable persons and residents or residential-unit owners.
Disclosure may still be limited by data protection and lawful restrictions.
Registration asks for structure and fire-safety information for each structure where a building has more than one structure.
Structure boundaries must be determined from building-specific evidence.
The PAP should take all reasonable steps to find the requested key building information.
Reasonable steps do not guarantee that every field is known.
Recent fire-risk assessments, external-wall appraisals and maintenance or inspection records may contain key building information.
Existing records may be outdated, incomplete or outside their original scope.
KBI should describe the building as it is now or at the most recent survey, not planned changes or improvements.
The most recent survey date and subsequent changes must be checked.
Detailed structure and fire-safety information must be provided within 28 days after the registration application.
A deadline does not prove that the submitted information was timely or accurate.
KBI asks for the evacuation strategy for residential areas, with options including phased, progressive horizontal, simultaneous, stay put and temporary simultaneous.
A selected strategy must not be treated as suitable without the building's fire-risk context.
A temporary simultaneous strategy requires a later update when the strategy changes.
Temporary status does not establish when or whether the change occurred.
KBI asks whether residential units contain heat detectors, smoke detectors, sprinklers or misters, with an option for none or inaccessible units.
An inaccessible-unit response must not be interpreted as confirmed absence of equipment.
KBI asks about specified alarms, dampers, extinguishers, shutters, detectors, risers, smoke controls and sprinklers in shared parts.
The listed categories are not a complete inventory or a condition assessment.
For most reported fire and smoke equipment, KBI asks for locations such as basements, corridors, staircases, lobbies and rooftops.
A reported location does not verify operation, coverage or maintenance condition.
KBI distinguishes evacuation lifts, firefighters lifts and fire-fighting lifts using their functions and applicable standards.
A marketing label or ordinary passenger lift must not be assigned a protected lift class without evidence.
KBI asks for counts of residential front doors and common-part fire doors by certified resistance duration, including unknown classifications.
A certification category does not establish present door condition or installation quality.
KBI asks about site energy storage such as hydrogen or lithium-ion batteries, excluding storage that supplies individual residents' equipment.
The listed options are not a complete hazard inventory and do not establish condition.
KBI asks about on-site generation and building energy supplies, including heat pumps, biomass, solar or wind, communal heating, electricity, gas and oil.
Presence of an energy system does not establish safety, capacity or compliance.
KBI asks about visible external-wall materials and specified building works such as cladding, cavity barriers, added floors, rewiring and changes to fire systems.
Reported materials or works require source records and must not be inferred from imagery or age alone.
The wave39_bsr_ source-id prefix had no indexed repository match before publication.
